newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says won't give up new ties with Sao Tome.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says won't give up new ties with Sao Tome.

text.p: Taiwan on Saturday said it would not give up newly-established formal ties with West Africa's small twin-island nation of Sao Tome and Principe despite reports that Sao Tome's cabinet had rejected the new links.

"We have sent deputy director of (the foreign affairs ministry's) African affairs department to (Sao Tome) ... we will further realise the actual situation," Foreign Minister John Chang said on state television.
Chang made the comment after reports in local newspapers on Saturday said Sao Tome's cabinet has rejected its president's proposal to establish ties with Taiwan.
Taiwan announced on May 6 that it had established formal ties with Sao Tome, scoring a minor victory in its four-decade diplomatic tug-of-war with arch rival China.

The announcement brought to 31 the number of countries that maintain official relations with Taiwan's exiled Republic of China, although the number will fall back to 30 later this year when South Africa switches ties to communist China.
Chang attributed the changing factors on the new ties to China's taking action to try to stop the new relations.
"Since May 6, Chinese mainland has tried everthing it could to add changing factors on our new ties with Sao Tome, thus stirring disputes inside (Sao Tome)," Chang said on Saturday.
China said it was absolutely opposed to Sao Tome establishing diplomatic relations with Taiwan, but stopped short of saying it would sever official ties with the African republic.
Sao Tome had maintained diplomatic ties with Beijing before switching recognition to Taipei.
China has regarded Taiwan as a rebel province since a Chinese civil war split them in 1949, and has warned other counties against establishing ties with the island.
Sao Tome and Principe, a former Portuguese colony 200 km (125 miles) off the coast of Gabon, is one of the poorest countries in the world and heavily depends on foreign aid.
It became independent from Portugal in 1975, and in 1991 held its first presidential and mulit-partisan congress elections.
The African country has a foreign debt of US$340 million, which it is unable to finance, and desperately needs aid to fund development projects.

Nationalist Taiwan and China have competed aggressively, especially in Africa, for diplomatic recognition since 1949, often accusing each other of using large sums of cash and aid to woo potential backers.
In the past five years, another poor African nation, Niger, switched ties twice -- first to Taipei from Beijing in 1992 and then back to Beijing in 1996.
